newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business News - August 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business News - August 5.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- STORES FEAR CUSTOMERS WILL ABUSE EU RULES

High street retailers have complained new European Parliament proposals to give customers up to one year for any exchange, refund or repair on any purchase found to be faulty, could lead to increasing 'sale and return' abuses. The British Retail Consortium admits such abuses are rare at present, but under the new plans could be a much bigger problem and lead to price increases. European officials believe the proposals will improve the single market and encourage manufacturers to increase the quality of goods.
-- HARVEY NICKS CHIEF TIPPED FOR BARNEY'S

Hong Kong financier Dickson Poon is reportedly considering the transfer of Harvey Nichols' chief executive Joseph Wan to head of Barney's, the trendy New York department store which Poon recently took control of with a successful $322m bid. Wan has stated he is up for the challenge, but had not yet held any talks with Poon and is, either way, 'very comfortable' at Harvey Nicholls.
-- FLEXTECH CHIEF PUTS END TO TALK OF RESIGNATION

Flextech, the pay-TV provider, has denied reports its chief executive Roger Luard is to resign, as Luard expressed he remained 'committed to Flextech' and 'fully intends' to be involved in the company's continued growth and development. Luard recently sold 70,000 shares in the company, leaving him with 100,000 and options on a further 198,050, his first sale of company shares during his 12 years with Flextech.
THE TIMES
-- PEARSON PLANS TO DOUBLE MARKET VALUE IN FIVE YEARS

The Pearson media group has reported better-than-expected half-year results, including a pre-tax profit of 80.7m stg on sales up two per cent at 958m stg. Pearson chief executive Marjorie Scardino declared the group is aiming at a 1332p share price within five years, as the company will focus on revenues, margins and cash generation. Scardino added rumours of a feud with Greg Dyke were 'just not true', as were rumours the group is looking to dispose of Pearson TV.
-- SHIRE PAYS 113M STG FOR US NETWORK

Andover-based Shire Pharmaceuticals has acquired Richwood Pharmaceuticals of the US for 113.3m stg, its second major US acquisition in the year, which is hoped to give the group a US distribution network for its existing drugs. Shire are best known for their work in the market for treating hyperactive children, as is Richwood, which recently launched the Adderall hyperactivity treatment. The purchase will be funded through an 088.9m stg share issue.
-- COUNTRY CASUALS SPURNS SUITORS TO GO IT ALONE

Womens clothing designer and retailer Country Casuals on Monday disclosed it has rejected all of its remaining suitors, an announcement which caused shares in the group to fall 20p to 113p. Company chairman Tom Adam refused to comment on the latest potential buyers, but it is believed they were other women's wear retailers. Adam did state, however, the company's first half same-store sales were up eight per cent.
THE GUARDIAN
-- TELEWEST IN 1.9BN STG CABLE EMPIRE TALKS

On Monday, NTL and Telewest confirmed they had entered talks which could result in the creation of a 1.9bn British cable company, the country's second largest. While talks are in their preliminary stages, the strategy of the two groups has become apparent, with NTL having indicated it is looking to create a company similar to the 4.3bn stg Cable & Wireless Communications group.
-- BRITISH DON'T BUY SHOPPING THEORY

Research from the National Consumer Council has shown less British people are visiting the country's shops in 1997 than five years ago during the recession. The survey also reveals when they do visit shops, Britons complain of rude and unhelpful staff, combined with a lack of open check-outs. Shop workers union Usaw has blamed the increase in customer complaints on employers' obsession with profits, lack of training and poor salaries.
-- APPLE FOUNDER JOBS SEEKS CHIEF TO SECOND-GUESS

On Wednesday, Apple's current leader Steve Jobs is to make one of the company's most significant speeches, when he addresses the Mac World Expo trade show in Boston. The speech is hoped to restore shareholders' faith in the group, though it is uncertain who, if anyone, Jobs will name to the company's board or appoint as chief executive, or whether or not Jobs will reveal plans for a new version of the Macintosh operating system.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- BRITISH GAS TRIUMPHS IN DOMESTIC TRIALS

A survey commissioned by the Electricity Association has revealed British Gas was successful in retaining the majority of its customers despite recent trials of domestic competition. The survey shows only low-paying households abandoned British Gas, serving a blow to the independent providers as trials were held in one of the UK's most prosperous areas. A similar survey from Cornwall, Devon and Somerset reveals more than one third of customers who switched from British Gas were overcharged.
-- ZENECA'S SCHIZOPHRENIA DRUG APPROVED

The Zeneca pharmaceuticals group has received approval from the UK Medical Control Agency to market its antipsychotic drug, Seroquel, used in the treatment of schizophrenia. The MCA announcement follows similar approval which was given by the US Food and Drug Administration last week and represents Zeneca's first entry into the antipsychotic market, furthering its range of drugs used to treat central nervous system disorders.
-- GALAXY CHIEF OUSTED WITHOUT PAYOFF

John Webber has been ousted as chief executive of the Galaxy Media Corporation, without compensation, in a move company vice-chairman and leading shareholder Christopher Moran attributed to a significant shift in the company's planned future development. Galaxy is currently seeking to concentrate its business in film, TV, music and stage promotions, along with management of sporting events and artists.
